title: Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard -- Ch. 7: Warrantless Arrests and Seizures Revisited
keywords: Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard
Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr.
Section 5, Rule 113 of the Rules of Court
primary_topics: Chapter 7 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' -- a restatement, through CJP's Concurring Opinion in People v. Doria, of the doctrines governing warrantless arrests, warrantless searches and the Miranda rights, offered as a practical guide for law enforcers, judges and lawyers.

The correction of People v. Montilla: the Court's unanimous return in Doria to the original principles on illegal arrests, effectively reversing the obiter that the doctrines should be relaxed to be of understanding assistance to law enforcement agencies.

The insistence that in both in flagrante delicto and hot pursuit arrests the arresting officer must have personal knowledge of the commission of an offense, so that suspicious appearance, informants' tips and raw intelligence will not do.

The enumeration and strict construction of the six permissible warrantless searches and of the eleven Mahinay guidelines for custodial investigation, framed by the premise that any exception to the warrant requirement must be strictly construed in favor of liberty.
sub_topics: The opening observation that apparently guilty persons are acquitted to the disappointment of law enforcers and the pained cries of victims, mostly because police violated the accused's rights against illegal arrests and seizures.
CJP's admission that the law and jurisprudence on these subjects are not easy to understand and that even judges and lawyers disagree on their scope.
The general rule that no person may be arrested and no search conducted without a warrant, and the problem posed when immediate action is needed.

The Montilla majority's view, recalled from Battles in the Supreme Court, that existing doctrines should be relaxed, and the unanimous Doria ruling through Justice Puno that an arrest is legally objectionable absent the arrester's own knowledge of implicating facts.
CJP's Concurring Opinion in Doria, written to outline guidelines on when an arrest or search without a warrant is valid, covering warrantless arrests, warrantless searches and the Miranda rights.
Section 5 of Rule 113 quoted in full, with the focus placed on paragraphs (a) and (b), the two most frequently misapplied.
The two concurring elements of an in flagrante delicto arrest: an overt act indicating the crime, done in the presence or within the view of the arresting officer.

Malacat v. Court of Appeals, through Chief Justice Davide, holding that fast-moving eyes and looking at approaching persons did not justify arrest or search, and People v. Mengote, rejecting darting eyes and a hand over the abdomen.
Aminnudin and Encinada: appellants arrested while merely descending a gangplank on an informant's tip, their arrests invalidated because nothing in their conduct indicated a crime.

CJP's disagreement with Justice Regalado in Montilla, where the appellant was merely alighting from a passenger jeepney with a traveling bag and carton; what finally nailed him down was his implied waiver.

The two elements of a hot pursuit arrest -- an offense in fact just committed and the officer's personal knowledge of facts indicating who committed it -- with personal knowledge defined as actual belief or reasonable grounds based on actual facts.
People v. Burgos, where information from the civilian Masamlok was held not to be the lawmen's personal knowledge, and Encinada, where raw intelligence information was held insufficient.
Umil v. Ramos distinguished: subversion and rebellion as continuing offenses anchored on an ideological base, unlike common offenses that end upon commission.

The consequence that items seized after an unlawful arrest -- even marijuana or an unlicensed firearm -- are inadmissible, and the quoted passage from Burgos on strictly construing exceptions to the warrant requirement.
The six allowable warrantless searches enumerated: incident to lawful arrest, plain view, moving vehicles, customs searches, consent, and stop and frisk.
Search incident to lawful arrest under Section 12 of Rule 126, limited to the person of the arrestee at the time and place of apprehension.

The three requisites of the plain view doctrine and the practicability rationale for searching moving vehicles, with the extended American passage on automobiles as swift and powerful vehicles of silent approach and swift escape.
Customs searches under the Tariff and Customs Code, and consent searches, which must be express, knowing and voluntary rather than mere passive conformity, as illustrated by People v. Lacerna.

Stop and frisk, its American origin in Terry v. Ohio, its strict limits, and its valid application in Posadas and Manalili, where red eyes and a wobbly walk near a known drug hangout justified investigation.

The eleven Mahinay guidelines on informing an arrested person of the reason for arrest, the right to silence and counsel, free counsel, the conditions of a valid written waiver, the right to communicate, and the inadmissibility of evidence obtained in violation.
CJP's assessment that Doria and Mahinay were the most significant cases of his fourth year in defining the rights of persons under custodial investigation.
The closing exhortation from his own decision that courts have no right to expect ordinary people to be law-abiding if they do not insist on the full protection of their rights.

stances.claim: Doria rightly brought the Court back to well-settled doctrines on warrantless arrests and searches, which had seemingly been modified by an obiter in Montilla.
stances.rhetorical_move: vindication of an earlier dissent: describing the later unanimous ruling as a restoration rather than a change

stances.claim: In both kinds of warrantless arrest the officer must have personal knowledge of the commission of an offense; suspicious appearance, an informant's tip or raw intelligence information can never supply it.
stances.rhetorical_move: element-by-element restatement of the rule, each element anchored to a decided case

stances.claim: Montilla could not have been perceived as committing a crime while merely alighting from a jeepney carrying a traveling bag and a carton; what actually sustained his conviction was his implied waiver of objection to the arrest.
stances.rhetorical_move: respectful disagreement with a senior colleague, followed by reducing the majority's holding to an obiter

stances.claim: All the exceptions to the warrant requirement must be strictly construed, with every person's fundamental right to liberty and security kept foremost in mind.
stances.rhetorical_move: closing rule of construction, reinforced by a quoted passage on the strict construction of arrest exceptions

stances.claim: Glossing over an illegal search because the evidence of crime is produced condones law-breaking in the name of law enforcement and hastens the breakdown of the justice system, for the end never justifies the means.
stances.rhetorical_move: consequentialist warning to lawmen, prosecutors and judges, quoted from his own decision as a peroration

notable_anecdotes: CJP's recollection of writing a Dissent in People v. Montilla, recorded in his earlier book Battles in the Supreme Court, and of seizing the opportunity a year later to write a Concurring Opinion in Doria expressing relief at the Court's return to settled doctrine.

The police justification in Malacat that the appellant's eyes were moving very fast and were looking at every approaching person, which the Court through CJ Davide found insufficient even to elicit suspicion.
The Mengote arrest justified by the suspect's darting eyes and a hand over his abdomen, which the Court said could by no stretch of the imagination indicate a crime.
The Aminnudin and Encinada arrests of passengers simply descending a ship's gangplank on an informant's tip, invalidated because to all appearances they were not committing a crime.

Umil v. Ramos, where a suspected NPA member was arrested while being treated for a gunshot wound in a hospital and the Court held that he did not cease to be a subversive simply because he was confined.

Manalili, where members of the Caloocan City Anti-Narcotics Unit on surveillance saw a man with red eyes walking in a wobbly manner along a city cemetery known as a hangout of drug addicts, and the frisk was upheld.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 7 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' revisited the rules on warrantless arrests and seizures, beginning with Justice Panganiban's observation that apparently guilty persons are often acquitted because police violated the accused's constitutional rights, and his admission that the governing law is not easy to understand even for judges and lawyers. He recalled his Dissent in People v. Montilla, where the majority suggested that the doctrines on illegal arrests be relaxed so the Court could be of understanding assistance to law enforcement, and reported that a year later People v. Doria, written by Justice Puno, unanimously restored the original principles, holding the arrest of Gaddao and the consequent search illegal. He then reproduced his Concurring Opinion in Doria, written to guide law enforcers. Quoting Section 5 of Rule 113, he stressed that in both in flagrante delicto and hot pursuit arrests the officer must have personal knowledge of the commission of an offense: an overt act done in the officer's presence, as Malacat and Mengote showed, is not supplied by fast-moving eyes, darting looks or a hand over the abdomen, nor, as Aminnudin, Encinada and Burgos showed, by an informant's tip or raw intelligence information; Umil v. Ramos was distinguished as involving the continuing offenses of subversion and rebellion. Items seized after an unlawful arrest, he wrote, are inadmissible even when contraband. He then enumerated the six allowable warrantless searches -- incident to a lawful arrest, plain view, moving vehicles, customs searches, consent, and stop and frisk -- setting out the requisites of each, quoting the American rationale for vehicle searches and Terry v. Ohio for stop and frisk, and noting Lacerna, Posadas and Manalili. He added the eleven guidelines laid down in People v. Mahinay on custodial investigation, called Doria and Mahinay the most significant cases of his fourth year, and closed with a passage from his own decision warning that courts cannot expect people to be law-abiding if they do not insist on the full protection of rights, since the end never justifies the means.
